name: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP)
lead: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a yellow crystalline industrial chemical that has been used in explosives, pesticides and dyes, and that was briefly sold as a weight-loss drug in the United States in the 1930s [1]. It acts as a mitochondrial uncoupler: it makes cells release energy as heat rather than storing it as ATP, which raises metabolic rate [1][3].

In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums, DNP is discussed as a very fast fat-loss compound for getting leaner and showing more muscle definition and facial leanness, and users on looksmax.org describe cutting cycles lasting from a couple of weeks to a few weeks, often alongside other compounds [2][4][6]. It is not approved as a medicine, and is sold online as an industrial or research chemical [1].

Toxicology literature and regulators describe a narrow gap between amounts that raise metabolism and amounts that cause dangerous overheating (hyperthermia), and there is no specific antidote [1][12]. A prodrug of DNP designed to release it more gradually in the liver has been tested in a randomised phase 2a trial in people with fatty liver disease, and academic interest in low-level uncoupling for other conditions continues [1][13][14].

chain: Uncouples mitochondria so cells release fuel energy as heat
Raises metabolic rate and body temperature
Faster fat loss, so a leaner, more defined look
angle.text: Users take DNP to lower body fat quickly before photos, events or a season, expecting a leaner jaw, face and abdomen as fat drops. Forum members typically pair it with a calorie deficit and describe the scale weight falling within days, with part of the early change attributed to water.

infobox: Dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient as heat [1]
Not approved for human use; UK regulated poison since 2023; WADA-banned since 2015 [1]
Dinosan, Dnoc, Solfo Black, Nitrophen, Aldifen, Chemox [1]

paras: DNP is a small aromatic compound containing two nitro groups. Industrially it has served as a precursor in dyes and as a component of wood preservatives, pesticides and explosives, and it is classified as an explosive in the United States when dry [1]. Its use as a diet agent depends on a single biochemical property: it is a lipid-soluble weak acid that can cross the inner mitochondrial membrane carrying protons [1][3].

Among people who use it for appearance, DNP is typically described as a short-term cutting tool rather than a long-term drug. In forum logs it is run for a limited number of days or weeks, often with a low-calorie diet, and members track weight, water retention and body-fat changes in daily posts [2][4][9]. Users commonly describe it alongside other fat-loss compounds such as clenbuterol, tirzepatide and retatrutide [6][8].

Normally, the respiratory chain pumps protons out of the mitochondrial matrix, and the resulting gradient drives ATP synthase. DNP is a protonophore: it carries protons back across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase, so the energy from burning fuel is released as heat instead [1][3][13]. The body compensates by oxidising more fuel, which is the basis of the fat-loss effect. A general reference describes energy expenditure rising by roughly 30 to 40 percent [1].

A 1981 paper on DNP's mechanism of action is among the older primary-literature descriptions of this uncoupling effect, and a physiologically based pharmacokinetic model for DNP was published in 2022, reflecting continued academic interest in its behaviour in the body [5][13].

Because the toxicity of DNP is tied to how quickly it reaches high blood levels, researchers have developed a liver-targeted prodrug called HU6, which is converted to DNP in the liver and was designed to give more stable concentrations [1][14]. This line of work is pursued by drug developers rather than by the forum communities, but it is cited as evidence that the underlying idea of uncoupling for metabolic disease is still under investigation.

subs.h: Industrial origins and World War I
paras: DNP was linked to illness and some deaths among munitions workers in France during World War I [1]. A published toxicology review counts a series of 36 deaths among munitions workers in Paris reported in 1919 as the largest single series, and records that occupational deaths later fell after factory and legislative changes [12].

In 1933 the Stanford researcher Maurice Tainter published results in which obese patients treated with DNP lost an average of about 20 pounds, and most did not report adverse effects. In 1934 he estimated that at least 100,000 people in the United States had been treated in the first year, with three reported deaths [1]. Weight loss of up to about 1.5 kg per week has been described in the 1930s clinical reports [12].

In 1935 the American Medical Association's Council on Chemistry and Pharmacy declined to list DNP, judging its risks to outweigh benefits, and cataract reports emerged that year [1]. In 1936 a San Francisco ophthalmologist estimated that 2,500 American women had gone blind from DNP use, and some DNP was sold as a cosmetic to avoid drug rules [1]. The 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act expanded FDA authority, and DNP was deemed too toxic for human consumption [1][12]. In 1948 Loomis and Lipmann described its mechanism of action [1].

Texas physician Nicholas Bachynsky, who supplied DNP to patients under the name Mitcal, was convicted of drug offences in 1986 and of fraud in 2008 [1]. Prescribing had stopped after 1938 and fatalities became rare until the 2000s, after which published deaths were linked to deliberate overdose, bodybuilding or weight-loss use, and occupational exposure [12]. Use outside medicine increased in the 21st century as DNP became easy to find online, with users profiled as bodybuilders, fitness enthusiasts and people with eating disorders, a profile resembling that of anabolic steroid users [1].

sections.h: Use in appearance and bodybuilding culture

paras: Online accounts describe DNP being used for a limited period to cut before a competition, a photo shoot or a season. Tablets and capsules are the usual form, and Wikipedia notes that DNP has been sold alongside steroids or thyroid hormone and found as a contaminant in supplements [1].

A long-running T Nation guide thread, first posted in 2009, collected members' practices: running DNP in cycles with a specific diet, tracking weight and water, and focusing on hydration, electrolytes and avoiding heat [9]. The same thread opens with a bold warning that the main side effect is death by overheating, and members debated whether the forum should pin it, with some arguing that a pinned thread might look like endorsement [9]. Earlier T Nation discussions from 2007 and 2008 cited the toxicology literature on fatal cases, including a 2006 report of two deaths attributed to DNP [7].

DNP appears on looksmax.org in cutting logs, source-request threads and stack discussions with other fat-loss compounds [2][4][6][8][11]. Posters compare it with GLP-1-type compounds and share diets used alongside it. Reactions in threads range from enthusiastic to alarmed; one reply to a log said the compound was known to be fatal, while the poster said it was manageable with hydration [2]. Another poster argued that a testosterone plus retatrutide plan with a structured diet would outperform DNP [3].

The best-documented efficacy data are historical: the 1930s clinical reports of weight loss in obese patients, with an average metabolic-rate increase of about 11 percent described in a toxicology review [1][12]. No modern randomised controlled trial of DNP itself for fat loss was identified. Forum users report rapid weight loss; for example, one looksmax.org poster reported losing about 19.6 lb in 15 days while eating little, and another reported losing 8 to 10 lb of fat over 21 days alongside a calorie deficit and other compounds [2][6]. These are self-reports without controls, and some forum participants themselves note that part of the early drop is water [9].

subs.h: Effects reported in therapeutic and acute use
paras: DNP is described as having a low therapeutic index, meaning toxic exposures are not far above those that produce effects [1]. Reported effects include rash, yellow discoloration of skin, neuropathy, agranulocytosis, cataracts (sometimes with permanent vision loss), and rarely deafness [1][12]. Overdose is described as causing nausea, profuse sweating, tachycardia, rapid breathing and uncontrolled hyperthermia, with body temperatures reaching 44 degrees C in fatal cases [1][12].

In a 2013 toxicology review, symptoms began within hours, the average time to death in published acute-overdose cases was around 14 hours, and death was usually from cardiovascular collapse, sometimes with generalised rigidity [12]. A summary of poison-centre data for 2010 to 2020 reported an 11.9 percent fatality rate and at least 50 deaths worldwide in that period [1]. Animal studies have found teratogenic, mutagenic and carcinogenic effects [1].

The toxicology review states that no specific antidote exists. Management described in case reports and expert opinion consists of observation for at least 12 hours, external cooling with cooled fluids, control of seizures and agitation, and treatment of complications such as methaemoglobinaemia; it notes that dantrolene has been used in a single case report without supporting evidence [12].

Users on looksmax.org describe the heat and fever in the early days of a cycle, lethargy and sickness during use. One poster reported unbearable heat and fever by day 6 and skipped doses [2]. In the T Nation guide thread, commenters noted that some people who posted logs stopped posting after problems, and one described a member who stopped after a serious reaction [9].

In the United States DNP is classified as an explosive, is not approved as a drug, and has been designated an orphan drug for Huntington's disease [1]. In the United Kingdom a seller was convicted of manslaughter in 2018; the Court of Appeal ordered a retrial and in 2020 he was convicted of gross negligence manslaughter [1]. The UK government announced in January 2023 that it would reclassify DNP as a poison, effective October 2023, and the Home Office said it could not identify any legitimate industrial uses in the UK [1]. Australia lists it in Schedule 10 (a dangerous substance), Brazil in its prohibited-substances list, and in many jurisdictions it may be sold for non-consumption purposes [1].

The World Anti-Doping Agency has banned DNP since 2015, and Interpol and WADA issued an orange notice warning that year [1]. UK publicity campaigns in the early to mid 2010s are credited by some researchers with reducing use, while other researchers have argued that awareness campaigns could increase it [1]. A 2020 letter in the Medical Journal of Australia examined DNP exposures and deaths after Australia's 2017 up-scheduling [15].

Press coverage of DNP centres on young people who died after buying it online as a slimming or bodybuilding aid and on the prosecution of sellers; Wikipedia's account cites news reports on UK deaths and on the 2018 and 2020 convictions [1]. Poison-centre statistics for 2010 to 2020 recorded more overdose reports in Australasia, Europe and North America than elsewhere [1].

A 2019 review in Cells by a researcher who founded a company holding DNP-related patents argues that DNP at much lower, weight-neutral exposures might be reconsidered for neurodegenerative conditions, metabolic disease and ageing, by lowering reactive oxygen species and calcium overload; the author discloses the commercial interest, and the proposals remain hypotheses [3]. The same review notes the FDA granted an open investigational new drug application for early human testing [3].
No studies found for DNP itself as a modern fat-loss treatment. Historical 1930s clinical reports are summarised above [1][12].

A related trial tested HU6, a prodrug converted to DNP in the liver. In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial of 80 adults with fatty liver disease and BMI 28 to 45, once-daily HU6 for 61 days reduced liver fat on MRI by 27 to 36 percent relative to baseline across three dose groups versus a 5 percent increase on placebo. No serious adverse events were reported; flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were the commonest effects. The trial was funded by the developer [14].
Laboratory research has examined DNP in cell models of neurodegeneration, in which a 2024 study reported protective effects against okadaic acid toxicity in cultured cells [10].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org DNP is discussed as a rapid fat-loss compound used for cutting before events or at the start of a season, usually stacked with other compounds, and members trade experience logs and source requests [2][4][6]. On T Nation it has been discussed since at least 2007, with a mix of harm-reduction guides and warnings [7][9].

claims.claim: DNP is a "super effective cut" that produces about 8-10 lb of fat loss in three weeks.
claims.believers: Users report large short-term weight drops, such as roughly 19.6 lb in 15 days, with little or no training, attributing it to the compound [2][6].
claims.experts: Mechanistic literature agrees that uncoupling raises energy expenditure and 1930s clinical reports recorded weight loss, but no modern controlled trial has quantified fat loss with DNP, and scale weight can include water [1][12].

claims.claim: The risks are manageable with hydration, avoiding heat and electrolyte attention.
claims.believers: Posters say they completed multi-week cycles and that side effects such as heat and fever faded after adjustments; some guides present hydration and heat avoidance as the key safeguards [2][9].
claims.experts: Toxicology sources describe a narrow therapeutic index, no antidote, fatal hyperthermia, and an 11.9 percent fatality rate in poison-centre reports from 2010 to 2020 [1][12].

claims.claim: Testosterone plus retatrutide and a structured diet outperforms DNP, so DNP is unnecessary.
claims.believers: Some members argue modern peptides, low-dose testosterone and aggressive calorie control give comparable results with fewer dangers [3].
claims.experts: No published head-to-head comparison between DNP and these combinations was found.

claims.claim: DNP can be sourced online from supplement vendors or EU suppliers.
claims.believers: Members regularly ask for and share sources, including in Europe [6][11].
claims.experts: In the UK it is a regulated poison since 2023, a seller has been convicted of manslaughter, and WADA bans it [1].

claims.claim: Part of the quick weight drop is water, so DNP logs overstate fat loss.
claims.believers: Some forum guides and log-readers themselves say early results are partly water loss and that body-fat tracking is needed [9].
claims.experts: No controlled study separates fat from water change in recreational DNP use.

claims.claim: Low-level uncoupling could have medical uses beyond weight loss, so DNP's bad reputation is overstated.
claims.believers: Proponents of uncoupler medicine, including the author of a 2019 review, argue low weight-neutral exposures might help brain, liver and metabolic conditions [3].
claims.experts: A liver-targeted prodrug lowered liver fat in a phase 2a trial; the review's author discloses a commercial interest, and DNP itself is not approved for any use [3][14].

card.summary: A 1930s diet drug that melts fat by turning cells into heaters; the narrow gap between effective and lethal is why it is banned for human use.
card.note: Fatal overheating with no antidote; regulated poison in the UK since 2023; banned by WADA.

quick.overview:
DNP is an industrial chemical that was sold as a diet pill in the 1930s before being judged too toxic. It reappeared in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles as a very fast fat burner, with users reporting several pounds lost per week.

Evidence for its fat-loss effect is historical and anecdotal; no modern controlled trials exist. The mechanism is well understood, but the safety margin is described as very narrow.
quick.mechanism: DNP shuttles protons across the mitochondrial membrane, so cells burn fuel and release the energy as heat instead of making ATP. Metabolic rate rises, and so does body temperature.
quick.risks: Reported harms include overheating (hyperthermia) up to fatal temperatures, cataracts, rash, and blood and organ damage. There is no antidote. It is not approved for human use; the UK made it a regulated poison in 2023, a seller has been convicted of manslaughter, and WADA bans it.
